questions.question: You're halfway through a feature when an urgent bug comes in. You don't want to commit unfinished work. How do you set your changes aside and get a clean working tree?
questions.explanation: `git stash` saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) on a stack and resets your files to the last commit. Fix the bug, then bring your work back with `git stash pop`. `reset --hard` and `restore .` would throw the changes away.

questions.question: What is the difference between `git stash pop` and `git stash apply`?
options: `pop` applies the stash and removes it from the list; `apply` applies it and keeps it
`apply` applies it and removes it; `pop` only shows it
`pop` applies the oldest stash; `apply` the newest
questions.explanation: `apply` is useful when you want the same changes on several branches. Remove an entry later with `git stash drop`, or all of them with `git stash clear`.

questions.question: You ran `git stash`, but your new file `helpers.py` is still in your working tree. Why, and what should you have run?
options: By default stash skips untracked files; use `git stash -u`
Stash only saves staged changes; use `git stash --all-files`
Stash only works on Python files after `git add`
questions.explanation: `-u` (`--include-untracked`) also stashes new files. `-a` (`--all`) goes further and includes ignored files. Alternatively, `git add helpers.py` first, because staged new files are stashed.

questions.question: Which command shows all the stashes you've saved?
questions.explanation: Each entry is named `stash@{0}` (newest), `stash@{1}`, and so on, with the branch and commit it was made on. Stashes are local only; they're never pushed.

questions.question: You have several stashes and can't tell them apart. How do you save the next one with a description?
questions.explanation: `git stash push -m` adds a message that shows in `git stash list`. `git stash save 'msg'` is the older, deprecated form. Plain `git stash` is short for `git stash push`.

questions.question: `git stash list` shows three entries and you need the oldest one, `stash@{2}`, without removing it. Which command?
questions.explanation: Both `pop` and `apply` take a stash name and default to `stash@{0}`. Newer versions of Git also accept just the number: `git stash apply 2`.

questions.question: Before applying a stash, you want to see exactly which lines it changes. Which command?
questions.explanation: `git stash show` gives a `--stat` summary, and `-p` shows the full patch. A stash is stored as a commit, so `git diff stash@{0}` works too, but it compares it with your current working tree.

questions.question: You changed five files but want to stash only `config.yml`. Which command?
questions.explanation: `git stash push` accepts paths after `--`. `git stash push -p` lets you pick changes chunk by chunk, like `git add -p`.

questions.question: `git stash pop` runs into a merge conflict. What happens to the stash entry?
options: It stays in the stash list; drop it yourself after resolving the conflict
It's dropped, and the conflict is all that remains
It's turned into a commit on the current branch
The pop is cancelled and nothing in your files changes
questions.explanation: Git prints "The stash entry is kept in case you need it again." Resolve the conflict, `git add` the file (or `git restore --staged` it if you don't want it staged), and run `git stash drop` once you're sure.

questions.question: A stash from weeks ago no longer applies cleanly to your branch. Which command applies it on a new branch that starts at the commit where the stash was made?
questions.explanation: `git stash branch` creates the branch at the stash's original commit, applies the stash there (where it always fits), and drops it if that works. Then merge or rebase that branch as usual.

questions.question: You're mid-way through a big change and need to fix a bug on `main` **at the same time**, in a separate folder, without stashing or cloning again. Which command?
questions.explanation: A worktree is an extra working folder linked to the same repository: same history, different checked-out branch. One branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time. Remove it when you're done with `git worktree remove ../shop-hotfix`; `git worktree list` shows them all.

questions.question: Which command deletes **all** your stashes at once?
questions.explanation: `git stash clear` empties the list without asking. `git stash drop` removes one entry (the newest by default). Use them carefully: dropped stashes can only be dug up with `git fsck`, and only for a while.
